The United States has no federal proof-of-funds threshold for an F or M student visa. No federal figure was found on any government page I fetched. What is published is institution-specific: the Form I-20 is completed by the school, and the school certifies its own estimate of cost. The closest official document I could fetch confirms the opposite point — the Department of State directs students to the SEVP-approved school for the first step and to the SEVIS I-901 fee, with no money threshold stated — while the university pages I fetched state their own required total budget (for example Michigan Tech's USD 63,019 non-resident annual total, which is that institution's estimate, not a national requirement). Any specific I-20 amount must therefore be attributed to a named university rather than to the US government, and I did not fetch a university page that publishes a dedicated 'proof of funds' number separate from its cost-of-attendance budget. travel.state.gov returned HTTP 403 to every request, so the Department of State's student-visa document list could not be read directly.

Archived evidence recorded a finding with no numeric figure: USCIS lists no student-status route to a Green Card; permanent residence is reachable only through categories such as family, employment, special immigrant, refugee/asylee, humanitarian or registry, so there is no minimum study duration that confers permanent residence.

sources.notes: Michigan Tech is a single named US university, chosen because its own admissions page publishes a full, labelled breakdown. International (visa-holding) undergraduates are charged the non-Michigan-resident rate, plus a $250 per-semester international surcharge. The university-level tuition is USD 44,504 per year; mandatory fees add USD 1,095 (374 required fees + 621 lab and course fees + 100 from the two $250 semester surcharges for a two-semester year), and housing, food, books and personal costs are listed separately as budgeted expenses rather than billed tuition. These figures are university-set, not federal; they are not transferable to other US institutions.

sources.notes: The full category list fetched from USCIS contains no student-status or post-study route to a Green Card; there is no minimum-years-of-study pathway. Study in the US can only lead towards permanent residence indirectly, through an employment-based category (for example an EB-2/EB-3 worker or an EB-1 extraordinary-ability applicant), and to reach those the applicant must first hold a separate nonimmigrant work status such as H-1B. The fetched page publishes no minimum number of years, so the requested 'minimum years' figure is UNAVAILABLE and is not asserted. Category names and the employment-based structure above are quoted from the page.

sources.notes: USCIS is the issuing authority and this is its own OPT page, last reviewed 25 November 2024. Official permission name: Optional Practical Training (OPT) for F-1 students, requiring a DSO recommendation endorsed on Form I-20 plus a separate Form I-765 filed with USCIS. Hour caps: pre-completion OPT is limited to 20 hours or fewer per week while school is in session, full time when school is not; post-completion OPT requires at least 20 hours per week. Duration: up to 12 months at each educational level, with a further 24-month STEM OPT extension (36 months total per degree). On-campus employment rules were not captured from a fetched page and are not asserted.
